subject: Architecture
title: Embodied Carbon: The Hidden Footprint
description: A quick win: understand Embodied Carbon: The Hidden Footprint.

hook.text: Before anyone moves in, a new building has already emitted tons of carbon just from being built.

buildup.text: Embodied carbon counts the emissions from mining, manufacturing, transporting, and assembling materials.

discovery.text: Concrete and steel together account for about 15% of all human-caused carbon emissions worldwide.

twist.text: An energy-efficient building with high embodied carbon can be worse than a standard building that is reused.

climax.text: Architects now calculate whole-life carbon — both construction and operation — before designing anything.

punchline.text: The greenest building is the one you don't demolish.

quiz.question: What does 'embodied carbon' measure?
options: Carbon absorbed by trees planted around a building
Emissions from making, transporting, and assembling building materials
Carbon dioxide levels inside occupied buildings

details.summary: Embodied carbon is the total CO2 emitted during a building material's extraction, manufacturing, transport, and installation — before the building is even occupied.
details.whyItMatters: As operational energy efficiency improves, embodied carbon becomes the dominant emissions source. A highly efficient new building may take 30-80 years of operational savings just to offset the carbon emitted during its construction.
takeaways: Embodied carbon covers extraction, manufacturing, and installation
Concrete and steel produce roughly 15% of global CO2 emissions
Efficient buildings may need decades to offset construction emissions

faq.question: Which building materials have the highest embodied carbon?
faq.answer: Concrete (due to cement production) and steel (due to smelting) are the largest contributors by total volume used globally. Aluminum is extremely carbon-intensive per kilogram but used in smaller quantities.

faq.question: How can architects reduce embodied carbon?
faq.answer: Use less material through efficient structural design. Substitute high-carbon materials with lower alternatives like mass timber, recycled steel, or low-carbon concrete. Reuse existing structures instead of demolishing. Specify locally sourced materials to reduce transport emissions.
